subtitle: Leading an accessible organization means setting clear expectations and removing barriers. You will learn to make accessibility a routine part of ordinary leadership decisions.
scope: For leaders across DHS who shape work plans, services, staffing, purchasing and communications. The examples use DSD work, but the questions apply across programs and service lines. Use responsible agency offices for formal accessibility, accommodation and legal determinations.
introTranscript: An accessible organization allows people to use its services and take part in its work without repeatedly having to explain why a barrier matters. Leaders influence that experience through deadlines, budgets, purchasing and everyday expectations. This course follows a practice DSD team preparing a service-information update. You will examine the whole journey, distinguish accessible design from individual accommodation, set responsibilities, involve people respectfully, and decide what evidence you need before calling the work ready. The aim is practical leadership: listen, make room for expertise, and follow through on barriers you can address.

lessons.title: Start with the person’s whole journey
lessons.summary: A usable front door is only the beginning. Follow the task through information, action and a response.
lessons.objective: Map the steps a person takes to complete one DHS task and identify at least two possible barriers.
objectives: Map the steps a person takes to complete one DHS task and identify at least two possible barriers.
Distinguish a barrier in a service or work process from an assumption about a person’s ability.
Choose an accessibility improvement that preserves the person’s control over the task.
takeaways: Look at the complete task, including what happens after a person submits information.
A disability is not evidence that a person cannot use a service or do a job.
Ask how the process works for the person before deciding what support is useful.
lessons.statement: Accessibility is experienced as a connected journey. A clear webpage cannot compensate for an unusable form or a meeting that someone cannot join.

image.caption: People bring different ways of reading, communicating and participating to the same work.

intro.heading: Follow a real task from beginning to end
intro.body:
A person looking for waiver information might first hear about a service, read a webpage, open a document, contact a lead agency, complete a form and wait for a response. A staff member preparing that information might need to find a shared file, use an editing tool, attend a review meeting and approve the final copy. These are connected tasks. A barrier at any point can block the result even when the earlier steps work well.

Begin with the task rather than a list of disability categories. Can a person find the information, understand what it asks, operate the form and confirm what happens next? Someone may use a screen reader, magnification, captions, a keyboard, a support person or another method. A person may use several methods or change them over time. Do not assume that an adjustment suitable for one person will suit everyone with a similar disability.

In a practice DSD update, the team creates a readable announcement but links to a scanned form. A caller is told to ask a family member to complete it. That moves responsibility for the barrier onto the caller and may compromise privacy or independence. A better response is to arrange an effective way to complete the task now and correct the inaccessible form with the responsible staff.

As a leader, ask where a person could get stuck and who can fix that step. Do not diagnose people or collect medical histories for a journey review. Describe the obstacle: a control cannot be reached with a keyboard, the document’s reading order is confusing, or the next step is unclear. That description gives colleagues something to investigate and improve.

inThisLesson: Trace a service and an employee task.
Name barriers without judging a person.
Compare assistance with an accessible process.
Choose who should follow up on one blocked step.
lessons.keyStatement: Name what prevents the task, not what you assume is wrong with the person.

flashcards.back: The connected steps a person takes to reach a result, such as understanding a service and submitting a request.
A feature or practice that prevents equal participation, such as an unlabelled form control or a conversation without effective communication support.
Tools that support a person’s way of using information or equipment, such as a screen reader or speech input.
Having meaningful control over a task. A person can choose assistance without being forced to rely on it because the service is inaccessible.

items.title: Finding and understanding
items.body: Ask whether the person can locate the correct information and recognize the next step. Plain wording and accessible formats address different needs; neither substitutes for the other.

items.title: Completing and confirming
items.body: Test whether a person can enter information, correct an error and learn that it was received. Include the confirmation and later response in the review.

items.title: Preserving choice
items.body: Offering a support person may help, but requiring someone to disclose private information to a relative because a form is inaccessible is a different matter. Ask what effective options the person prefers.

tabs.heading: Three viewpoints on the same task

tabs.label: Person using a service
tabs.body: The person needs a reliable way to understand the choices and communicate their own decision. Ask about the task, not a presumed diagnosis.

tabs.label: Staff preparing the service
tabs.body: Staff need accessible authoring tools and time to test the final result. A late repair can be prevented when the team works from a usable template.

tabs.label: Leader reviewing the work
tabs.body: A leader connects barriers to owners and decisions. Ask for evidence of a working task, not only a declaration that the file looks professional.

check.question: A public form cannot be completed with a keyboard. Which response best addresses the barrier?
check.correct: Arrange effective access now and assign correction of the form, while asking what works for the person.
wrong: Tell the person to ask a relative to enter the information.
Record that people with disabilities cannot use online forms.
Make the webpage headline larger and leave the form unchanged.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This addresses the immediate task and the underlying barrier without assuming incapacity or imposing a helper.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Reconsider where the task stops. A cosmetic change or imposed helper leaves the obstacle in place and may reduce the person’s privacy or choice.

sorting.heading: Sort the description, not the person

items.text: The Submit button cannot be reached by keyboard.
The caller must be unable to make their own decisions.
What happens after a person sends the form?
The video contains spoken instructions but has no captions.
Anyone who needs assistance will want a family member involved.
Which way of receiving this information works for you?

lessons.next: The next lesson separates broad access responsibilities from an individual accommodation request so each reaches the right people.

scenario.context: In this example, a team’s waiver information is clear, but its attached form is a scanned image. A resident cannot read it with their screen reader. The team suggests waiting for the next annual update.
options: Provide an effective accessible route now, assign the document repair and check the complete task.
Wait for the annual update because the webpage itself is accessible.
Ask a relative to read the form and treat the issue as resolved.
responses: This addresses present access and prevents the same problem for the next person. The responsible staff still need to check the repaired form.
The linked form is part of the task. Waiting leaves the known barrier in place.
A person may choose assistance, but it does not replace the organization’s access responsibility.

lessons.transfer: Choose a practice or non-identifying task in your area. Write the first step, the final result and one step you have not yet checked.

move.control: You can choose which task your team reviews and who coordinates the review.
move.failure: A team checks only the landing page and misses the form, confirmation or follow-up.
move.next: Invite the relevant service and accessibility colleagues to test one complete journey.

lessons.title: Know which responsibility applies
lessons.summary: Accessible design, employment accommodation and public-service communication are connected, but their procedures differ.
lessons.objective: Distinguish broad digital accessibility work from an individual employment accommodation request.
objectives: Distinguish broad digital accessibility work from an individual employment accommodation request.
Identify when to involve the agency ADA Coordinator and when to involve digital accessibility staff.
Explain why a change in a federal deadline does not cancel Minnesota’s existing accessibility standard.
takeaways: Build accessible defaults and respond to individual needs.
Route a medical accommodation request promptly without requesting medical records yourself.
The Minnesota digital standard already applies; do not treat a later federal deadline as permission to pause.
lessons.statement: A broad access improvement helps many people. An individual accommodation responds to a particular person’s employment barrier. An organization needs both.

image.caption: Clear responsibilities help people get a useful response without repeating private information.

intro.heading: Match the issue to the right responsibility
intro.body:
Accessible design means planning tools, information and activities so people with disabilities can use them. Minnesota’s digital accessibility standard covers state digital information and technology and adopts WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA together with specified Section 508 requirements and state qualifications. A leader does not need to memorize every criterion, but does need to provide time, expertise and a clear process for applying the standard. A software label or a successful automated scan does not, by itself, prove that a complete task is accessible.

Employment accommodation is a separate responsibility. MMB Policy 1433 describes the process for qualified applicants and employees who need an adjustment because of disability. A request may arrive in ordinary words, without a form or the phrase reasonable accommodation. The recipient promptly forwards it to the appropriate decision maker and tells the person who that is. Supervisors must not request medical information or documentation; the agency ADA Coordinator handles appropriate documentation and formal questions.

Public services also have ADA Title II responsibilities, including effective communication and access to programs. A person asking for an accessible notice is not asking an employment accommodation question. Involve the appropriate agency accessibility or civil-rights staff rather than sending the person through a staff medical process.

Federal web and mobile accessibility deadlines are distinct from the state standard and from continuing ADA duties. Do not assume that a later compliance date means known barriers can be ignored. This lesson gives a way to direct the work, not a legal determination about a particular request. When responsibilities overlap, bring the responsible offices together and keep the person informed.

inThisLesson: Separate accessible defaults from individual requests.
Route an employment request promptly.
Recognize public-service communication needs.
Use current standards rather than an assumed deadline.
lessons.keyStatement: Route the issue by the task and responsibility, not by sending every person with a disability through the same process.

flashcards.back: A planned feature of ordinary work, such as an accessible meeting document, available without first asking a person to disclose disability.
An employment adjustment considered through the applicable process to provide equal opportunity for a qualified applicant or employee with a disability.
Communication that works for the person and the context. The method may differ with the nature, length and complexity of the information.
The designated agency official who supports the employment accommodation process and makes decisions outside delegated supervisor or manager authority.

items.title: A template that everyone uses
items.body: Ask the document owner and accessibility specialists to improve the template. Staff should not have to seek an individual accommodation each time a common document has the same avoidable flaw.

items.title: A request connected to a medical condition
items.body: Acknowledge it, promptly route it and explain who will respond. Do not demand a diagnosis or make a medical determination yourself. Follow the agency’s current process.

items.title: A member of the public who needs communication support
items.body: Arrange the appropriate agency response for effective communication. Consider the person’s requested method and the circumstances; do not substitute the employment accommodation procedure.

tabs.label: Employment
tabs.body: A staff member asks for an adjustment to perform a work task. Involve the designated accommodation decision maker and protect confidential information.

tabs.label: Public service
tabs.body: A resident needs an effective way to receive service information. The service owner works with the responsible accessibility or civil-rights staff.

tabs.label: Digital publishing
tabs.body: A team prepares an online form. Build to the state standard and test the actual journey before and after release. Individual support remains necessary when a person still encounters a barrier.

check.question: An employee says a medical condition makes a new work tool difficult to use. What should their supervisor do first?
check.correct: Acknowledge the request and promptly connect it to the appropriate accommodation decision maker without asking for medical records.
wrong: Ask the employee to send a full medical history to the whole team.
Wait until the employee uses the exact words reasonable accommodation.
Treat the new federal website deadline as permission to delay the response.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. An ordinary request can begin the process. Prompt routing and confidentiality are the supervisor’s responsibilities; medical documentation belongs with the ADA Coordinator.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A special phrase is not required. Avoid delays and medical-file collection. A public web deadline does not determine whether an employee’s request should be addressed.

items.text: Repair the headings in the team’s shared report template.
An applicant needs a disability-related adjustment for an interview.
A resident requests effective communication support for a service meeting.
Check keyboard operation in the new online form.
An employee requests a work adjustment because of a medical condition.
Provide an accessible format of a public notice in response to a resident’s need.

lessons.next: With the responsibilities clear, the next lesson puts them into budgets, schedules and ordinary work assignments.

scenario.context: A supervisor says every accessibility problem should go to HR. The communications team has discovered that a public form is unusable with a screen reader, and a staff member has separately requested a disability-related work adjustment.
scenario.prompt: What is the most useful direction?
options: Send both issues to HR and stop the communications review.
Assign the form repair to its owner with accessibility expertise, and promptly route the employee request through the accommodation process.
Tell the employee to use the public form’s feedback box.
responses: This would confuse responsibilities and leave the public task unaddressed. HR may be involved in employment matters but does not replace the form owner.
This separates the routes while allowing coordination where the work overlaps. Keep each affected person informed through the appropriate channel.
Public feedback is not a substitute for an employment accommodation response.

lessons.transfer: Without naming an employee, list the current contacts for digital accessibility, public-service access and employment accommodation in your area. Verify any contact you are unsure about.

move.control: You can make the routes clear and prevent requests from being passed between offices without ownership.
move.failure: Every issue is labelled an HR problem and service barriers remain unresolved.
move.next: Share the verified contacts with colleagues who receive requests and identify who follows up.

lessons.title: Make room in the plan and budget
lessons.summary: Accessibility improves when it has time, resources and an accountable owner before a deadline becomes urgent.
lessons.objective: Add accessibility work, expertise and review time to a project plan.
objectives: Add accessibility work, expertise and review time to a project plan.
Distinguish a genuine resource decision from an unsupported claim of undue hardship.
Assign one owner and a follow-up date to a known barrier.
takeaways: Plan accessibility when scope and budget are still open.
A local budget concern is not a supervisor’s unilateral accommodation denial.
Name who will act, what they will do and when you will check back.
lessons.statement: An expectation becomes workable when someone has the time, authority and resources to meet it.

image.caption: Planning accessibility with the team prevents avoidable pressure at the end of a project.

intro.heading: Turn a value into a workable commitment
intro.body:
Consider a practice DSD team revising service notices. The manager says accessibility is important but sets a deadline that allows only writing and visual review. Nobody has time to check document structure, keyboard use or the experience of receiving a notice in another format. When a barrier appears, it is treated as unexpected work. The problem began in the plan, before any file was created.

A more useful plan names the accessibility work beside writing, technical work and service review. It identifies the specialist time needed, the person who can approve changes, the point when checks happen and the room to repair problems. It also provides a way to respond while a barrier is being corrected. A leader may not personally repair a document or evaluate a tool, but can prevent the necessary expertise from becoming an unfunded favor.

Resource choices need careful boundaries. For employment accommodation, MMB Policy 1433 requires case-by-case consideration through the agency process. A supervisor cannot conclude that a request is an undue hardship simply because the team’s small discretionary budget is low. The policy directs consultation with the agency ADA Coordinator before denial and additional consultation for a denial based on lack of financial resources. Different legal responsibilities have their own decision rules; a course planning exercise does not establish an exception.

Start with a realistic commitment. Name the task, a responsible owner, support needed and a review date. Describe progress in terms of a person being able to complete the task. If an important decision exceeds your authority, route it to the person who can make it and remain responsible for tracking the response.

inThisLesson: Find the missing accessibility work in a plan.
Provide time for expertise and repair.
Recognize the limits of local budget authority.
Write an action with an owner and review date.
lessons.keyStatement: A deadline does not remove a responsibility; it makes early planning more valuable.

flashcards.back: The person responsible for coordinating a result and following its unresolved issues through the appropriate decision channels.
A planned moment to examine whether a person can complete the task and whether identified barriers were addressed.
An effective measure used while a longer repair is underway. Its suitability must be checked with the responsible staff and affected person.
A formal, case-specific accommodation question involving factors such as resources and operations. It is not simply an inconvenient purchase or an empty team budget.

accordion.heading: Three commitments a leader can make

items.title: Plan the expertise
items.body: Include the people who can examine documents, technology, procurement or communication needs before the scope is locked. Avoid assigning someone a specialist conclusion they cannot support.

items.title: Protect repair time
items.body: Schedule checks early enough for change. A review on the final afternoon may document a failure without leaving time to prevent it.

items.title: Keep responsibility visible
items.body: When a repair needs another office, write who received it and when the team will check back. Routing an issue does not mean it has been resolved.

tabs.label: People
tabs.body: Staff may need learning, specialist advice or protected time for testing. The responsible leader decides how that support fits the work plan.

tabs.label: Purchasing
tabs.body: A cost comparison should include configuration, testing, remediation and continuing support. A lower initial price does not establish an equally usable service.

tabs.label: Timing
tabs.body: A pilot can reveal barriers early, but pilot participants still need effective access. Do not use a pilot label to excuse known exclusion.

check.question: A supervisor says a requested disability-related adjustment is too expensive for the team’s remaining budget. Which response is sound?
check.correct: Consult the agency ADA Coordinator and follow the case-specific process instead of denying solely on the local budget.
wrong: Deny the request immediately because every team must balance its own budget.
Promise every requested adjustment without checking effectiveness or authority.
Ask coworkers to pay for the adjustment.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The policy requires proper consideration and consultation. You can raise resource concerns without turning them into an unsupported denial.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The issue needs the authorized accommodation process. Neither an immediate refusal nor an unexamined promise addresses effectiveness, resources and decision authority.

items.text: The document owner will test reading order before the review meeting.
We need the authorized office to decide the proposed exception.
Everyone should try to be accessible when they have time.
The manager schedules specialist review and a repair window.
The vendor has not explained how a known barrier will be corrected.
Accessibility is important, but it has no assigned time or owner.

lessons.next: The next lesson considers how leaders learn from people’s experience without placing all the work on them.

scenario.context: A practice notice project has a Friday deadline. Accessibility review finds a barrier on Wednesday. The leader knows a correction is needed, but the person who can authorize the change works in another office.
options: Mark the barrier resolved because it was forwarded.
Publish without a response and promise to revisit it next year.
Contact the decision maker, explain the blocked task, arrange effective access with the responsible staff and track the correction.
responses: Forwarding is a step, not a completed repair. A person remains responsible for following the decision.
This preserves the deadline by leaving people unable to complete the task. An unresolved access question needs attention now.
This connects the immediate need and the lasting repair without claiming authority you do not hold. The response and timeline still need confirmation.

lessons.transfer: For a non-identifying project, write one accessibility action with a responsible owner, required support and a review date. Name any decision that still needs another office.

move.control: You can reserve planning time, clarify responsibilities and raise resource decisions early.
move.failure: A broad promise substitutes for an actionable commitment.
move.next: Add one specific accessibility action to the next project discussion and confirm who owns it.

lessons.title: Learn from people without making them carry the program
lessons.summary: People’s experience helps reveal barriers. Participation should be respectful, accessible and voluntary where appropriate.
lessons.objective: Invite feedback about an access task without asking for unnecessary personal information.
objectives: Invite feedback about an access task without asking for unnecessary personal information.
Distinguish an individual’s experience from a claim about everyone with a disability.
Show how feedback changed a decision or explain what remains unresolved.
takeaways: Ask about the task and listen to the person’s preferred way of participating.
One participant does not represent every person with a similar disability.
Return to people with what changed and what still needs attention.
lessons.statement: Participation is most useful when people can influence a real decision and can see how their contribution was used.

image.caption: A respectful review makes room for different experiences without assigning anyone the role of speaking for everyone.

intro.heading: Listen with a clear purpose and a meaningful response
intro.body:
An accessibility review benefits from the experience of people who use the service or work process. A specialist can identify technical barriers, and a participant can show how the whole task works in practice. These perspectives complement each other. Neither a technical report nor one person’s successful experience establishes that every user will be able to complete the task.

Before inviting feedback, explain the decision, what remains open and how participation will occur. Offer accessible ways to respond. A long meeting with a dense document may exclude the people whose experience the team wants to understand. Ask what participation support is useful rather than requiring a diagnosis. Use the appropriate agency processes for compensation, public engagement and confidentiality; do not make promises that the team has not authorized.

The practice DSD team asks one colleague who uses a screen reader to approve the new notice. The colleague can provide valuable feedback but should not become the unpaid owner of all accessibility work or the spokesperson for everyone with a disability. Ask a focused question, provide the material in a usable form and leave technical verification with the responsible staff. Avoid turning a person’s willingness to help into an ongoing expectation.

Intercultural learning offers a related lens when culturally learned perspectives, values or communication practices are involved. In the Intercultural Development Continuum, Acceptance means understanding patterns of cultural difference and commonality, including how your own perceptions and behavior are culturally learned. Adaptation involves shifting cultural perspective and responding with culturally appropriate behavior. An accessibility improvement or an expression of empathy is not, by itself, evidence of either orientation. Use these ideas to examine cultural assumptions where relevant; do not infer an individual’s IDI result or rank participants. After a review, explain what changed, what could not yet be changed and who will follow up. A quiet feedback box without a response is not the same as participation in a decision.

inThisLesson: Prepare a focused invitation to contribute.
Make the feedback process accessible.
Avoid assigning one person a whole group’s perspective.
Close the conversation with a clear response.
lessons.keyStatement: Invite experience as expertise, then keep responsibility for the work with the people who own it.

flashcards.back: An opportunity to influence a decision while relevant choices remain open, with a clear explanation of how the contribution is used.
Knowledge from a person’s own experience. It is valuable without being a universal account of a whole group.

An intercultural orientation involving understanding patterns of cultural difference and commonality and examining one’s own culturally learned perceptions. General empathy or an accessibility improvement does not, by itself, establish this orientation.

An intercultural orientation involving a shift of cultural perspective and culturally appropriate behavior across differences. A general process change does not establish an individual’s orientation; the course does not assess IDI results.

items.title: Before the conversation
items.body: Share the task, the decision being considered and accessible materials. Explain what information will be recorded and avoid unnecessary identifying details.

items.title: During the conversation
items.body: Ask what worked, where the person stopped and what would help. Do not ask the person to justify their disability or speak for everyone.

items.title: After the conversation
items.body: Summarize what you heard, allow correction and describe the next action. Keep responsibility for technical and policy decisions with the appropriate staff.

tabs.label: Participant experience
tabs.body: The participant can describe the effect of a barrier and a preferred way to take part. They need not provide technical instructions for the repair.

tabs.label: Specialist review
tabs.body: A specialist checks the relevant requirements and the proposed correction. Specialist involvement does not make feedback from users unnecessary.

tabs.label: Leader follow-through
tabs.body: The leader decides how feedback changes the plan within their authority and explains the next step. Unresolved questions are recorded honestly.

check.question: One colleague successfully uses the revised form with a screen reader. What can the team conclude?
check.correct: The colleague’s experience is useful evidence, but broader task testing and specialist checks are still needed.
wrong: Every person with every disability can use the form.
The colleague is now responsible for every future accessibility review.
Technical testing is unnecessary because one person succeeded.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. A successful experience matters, but it supports a specific conclusion rather than universal approval. Keep the responsibility and remaining review clear.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Avoid extending one experience beyond what it shows. Different tasks, tools and needs may reveal other barriers, and the contributor is not automatically the program’s accessibility owner.

items.text: Could you show us where this task becomes difficult, if you want to participate?
Please explain your diagnosis to everyone before we discuss the form.
Your feedback led us to change the confirmation message; here is the next check.
Which way of reviewing the draft would work for you?
You use a screen reader, so please approve all our documents indefinitely.
The requested change needs another office; we will confirm its response with you.

lessons.next: The next lesson connects access expectations to purchasing and publishing decisions, where new barriers can be introduced.

scenario.context: A colleague volunteers to test one practice service form. The manager wants to name them as the team’s permanent accessibility approver because they have a disability.
options: Thank the colleague, confirm the limited voluntary contribution and keep specialist review and ownership with the responsible team.
Assign all future reviews to the colleague without discussing the role.
Stop asking for user feedback because one person cannot represent everyone.
responses: This respects the contribution and avoids transferring program responsibility based on disability. The team can still invite other relevant perspectives.
This turns a contribution into an assumed obligation and treats a disability as a job qualification without discussion.
Individual experience remains useful when its limits are understood. Combine it with other feedback and technical expertise.

lessons.transfer: Draft a two-sentence invitation about a practice task: what is open to change and how the person can choose to participate. Add a sentence explaining how you will respond.

move.control: You can make the purpose, participation choices and response clear.
move.failure: The team asks for stories but cannot show how any decision changes.
move.next: Invite focused feedback at a point when the team can still act and plan the return conversation.

lessons.title: Use purchasing and publishing as prevention points
lessons.summary: Before a tool or document becomes routine, leaders can ask for evidence that people can use it.
lessons.objective: Name accessible-use tasks for a proposed purchase or publication.
objectives: Name accessible-use tasks for a proposed purchase or publication.
Distinguish vendor statements and automated checks from evidence of usable tasks.
Choose a response to an unresolved barrier before committing to routine use.
takeaways: State the tasks people must be able to complete before selecting a tool.
A vendor’s accessibility report is evidence to examine, not a blanket guarantee.
Check changes and corrections after the initial purchase or release.
lessons.statement: Preventing a barrier is easier when access is part of the purchase and publication decision rather than a late request for a workaround.

image.caption: People who choose tools and prepare information influence access long before a user encounters a barrier.

intro.heading: Ask for evidence before committing
intro.body:
Purchasing and publishing decisions shape access for months or years. A reporting tool may be attractive but difficult to operate by keyboard. A template may look polished while giving a screen reader an illogical reading order. When either becomes the standard choice, the same barrier is repeated across many tasks. Leaders can prevent this by including accessibility in the requirements and review before the decision is final.

Start with the tasks. For a service tool, a person may need to sign in, find a record, enter information, correct an error and download a usable result. For a notice, a person may need to recognize its purpose, understand a deadline and act on the next step. Ask the appropriate accessibility and procurement staff how these tasks will be evaluated against the state standard and other applicable requirements. Do not invent an approval process or promise that the leader alone can waive a requirement.

Vendor statements and accessibility conformance reports can identify what the vendor says it tested and where limits remain. Examine the version, scope and exceptions. A report about a product is not necessarily evidence about your configured service, attachments or later updates. Automated checks also find only some problems. Combine relevant technical review with practical task testing and feedback.

In the practice DSD project, the team wants a low-cost form tool. Its demo works with a mouse but a key field cannot be reached with a keyboard. The leader asks for a correction and verified task evidence, and works with procurement and accessibility staff on the decision. A promise to fix the issue later needs a responsible owner and a real decision about present access. It does not itself establish that the tool is ready.

inThisLesson: Describe the tasks a purchase must support.
Read a vendor claim with attention to limits.
Ask for checks beyond appearance and automation.
Plan how changes will be reviewed.
lessons.keyStatement: A useful accessibility claim says what was tested, what remains and how the actual task works.

flashcards.back: A report describing how a product meets specified accessibility criteria and where it has limitations. Review its scope and evidence.
Trying a complete activity using relevant ways of interacting, rather than checking only the appearance of individual screens.
A specific access problem that has been identified and still needs correction or an authorized decision.
A check after an update or modification to ensure access has not been lost and repairs work as intended.

items.title: What are we buying or publishing?
items.body: Define the version, configuration, linked documents and user tasks. A report about a vendor’s demonstration may not cover the service the agency will actually use.

items.title: What evidence supports the claim?
items.body: Ask for relevant criteria, test results and limitations. Have the responsible specialists interpret the evidence rather than treating a badge as approval.

items.title: What happens if access fails?
items.body: Clarify the correction process, responsible contacts, response expectations and how effective access will be maintained. Procurement staff should address contractual terms through the authorized process.

tabs.label: Before selection
tabs.body: Include accessible use in the requirements and ask how it will be evaluated. Price and visual appeal do not substitute for access.

tabs.label: Before routine use
tabs.body: Verify the configured tasks and materials. Resolve known barriers with the responsible offices before assuming the service is ready.

tabs.label: After an update
tabs.body: Check changed tasks and previously corrected barriers. A product’s original report does not guarantee later versions.

check.question: A vendor provides an accessibility report but the agency’s configured form still has a keyboard barrier. What is the sound conclusion?
check.correct: The report is relevant evidence, but the actual barrier remains and needs correction or the appropriate authorized decision.
wrong: The report proves that no barrier can exist.
Keyboard use does not matter if mouse use is easy.
Any vendor report allows the leader to waive state requirements.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Evaluate the actual task and the report’s limits. The responsible staff need to address the problem; paperwork alone does not make it usable.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on what the person can do in the configured service. A report is not a waiver, and success with one way of interacting does not establish equal access.

items.text: A test record identifies the version and the keyboard tasks checked.
The vendor says the product is modern, so accessibility is assumed.
Recheck the form after the vendor’s proposed correction.
A report identifies supported criteria and known limitations.
The screen looks clean, so the document must read correctly.
Ask procurement and accessibility staff to review the unresolved issue.

lessons.next: The final lesson turns reviews and corrections into an ongoing leadership routine without claiming more than the evidence shows.

scenario.context: In this example, a team selects a service tool after a smooth demonstration. The vendor promises accessibility, but the team’s own test cannot complete the confirmation step using a keyboard.
scenario.prompt: What should the leader do next?
options: Ignore the result because the demonstration was successful.
Work with accessibility and procurement staff on the barrier and decision, and verify a correction in the configured task.
Require users who encounter the barrier to switch to a mouse.
responses: A demonstration does not outweigh an observed failure in the actual task.
This connects the evidence to the responsible decision process. The next check should show whether the correction works, not merely whether it was promised.
This imposes a method that may be unavailable to the person and leaves the barrier intact.

lessons.transfer: For a practice purchase or publication, list three complete tasks to test. Add one question about the scope of the vendor’s or author’s accessibility claim.

move.control: You can require relevant evidence and bring the proper specialists into the decision.
move.failure: A label or attractive demonstration replaces checking the actual service.
move.next: Review one upcoming purchase or publication for task evidence, known limits and a correction process.

lessons.title: Follow through without overclaiming progress
lessons.summary: Use a small set of meaningful checks to learn whether the work is becoming more accessible.
lessons.objective: Choose a measure that describes accessible task completion rather than training attendance alone.
objectives: Choose a measure that describes accessible task completion rather than training attendance alone.
Interpret missing evidence without calling it success.
Set a follow-up routine that protects personal information and revisits known barriers.
takeaways: Track whether a person can complete the task and whether repairs work.
No reported problem is not proof that no barrier exists.
Keep learning and accountability focused on the process, not on identifying or ranking staff by disability.
lessons.statement: Progress is a supported conclusion about a task or process, with remaining limits stated clearly.

image.caption: A team can learn from evidence while protecting people’s personal information.

intro.heading: Choose evidence that answers the access question
intro.body:
A leader needs to know whether a change made access better. Counting completed training can show that staff received learning, but it does not show that a service form works. Counting repaired files can show effort, but it does not establish that a person can complete the whole journey. Start with the question you want to answer: can people find the information, use the form and receive an understandable response through effective means?

A small review can combine a task check, a record of unresolved barriers and non-identifying feedback. Define what was checked, the period covered and the limits of the evidence. If nobody tested the confirmation step, mark it as unchecked. If no complaints were received, consider whether the feedback channel itself was accessible and known. Silence may reflect a good experience, but it may also reflect an unusable route or a person who gave up. Do not turn missing information into a positive conclusion.

Protect confidentiality. Employment accommodation records belong in the authorized process; medical information and the fact of an accommodation are confidential under MMB Policy 1433. A team accessibility review should not become a list of coworkers’ diagnoses or personal IDI results. Use non-identifying process information and consult the appropriate offices about any proposed reporting.

The practice DSD team sets a review after its revised notice is used. It checks the linked form, response and a repaired keyboard step, then records what worked and what still needs follow-up. The leader assigns the remaining action rather than grading the team as fully accessible. This is a useful rhythm: observe, correct, verify and learn. It keeps responsibility visible while making room for honest questions and further improvement.

inThisLesson: Match a measure to an access question.
Read missing evidence honestly.
Protect confidential accommodation information.
Plan a review of one corrected task.
lessons.keyStatement: A clear limit makes a conclusion more useful; it does not diminish the work that has been done.

flashcards.back: Information about how work is carried out, such as whether a repair has an owner and review date. It is not automatically evidence of a user’s result.
Evidence that a specified activity can be completed under the tested conditions. State those conditions and limits.
Information not yet collected or checked. It should remain unknown rather than being counted as success or failure without support.
Returning to an assigned action, confirming what happened and responding to unresolved barriers.

items.title: Choose one task
items.body: Name the complete activity and the ways of interacting that will be checked. Use the appropriate expertise to interpret the result.

items.title: Keep a short action record
items.body: Record the barrier, owner, action and review date without personal medical details. Describe an unresolved decision as unresolved.

items.title: Return to the result
items.body: Check the repair and invite relevant feedback. If it did not work, revise the action rather than declaring completion because the ticket closed.

tabs.label: Learning participation
tabs.body: Shows that people engaged with learning. It can support a capacity discussion, but does not prove a service meets accessibility requirements.

tabs.label: Technical and task review
tabs.body: Shows what criteria and activities were examined. A limited review needs a limited conclusion and follow-up for unchecked areas.

tabs.label: Feedback and complaints
tabs.body: Shows people’s reported experience through a particular channel. Look at whether that channel was accessible and understood before interpreting silence.

check.question: The team received no accessibility complaints, but nobody checked whether the feedback form is usable. What should the report say?
check.correct: No complaints were received through this channel; its usability still needs checking, so the absence does not establish full access.
wrong: The service is fully accessible to everyone.
The team must have failed because it received no complaints.
The lack of complaints removes the need for future checks.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This states the observation and its limit. Checking the channel and tasks is the next useful action.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Neither reassurance nor failure follows automatically from silence. State what is known and examine the missing evidence.

items.text: The tested form could be completed by keyboard under the recorded conditions.
All services are accessible because six staff finished a course.
Check whether the confirmation message works with a screen reader.
The corrected document’s reading order was verified in this review.
No complaint proves nobody encountered a barrier.
Ask whether the feedback route itself can be used.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to choose one task, name the responsible people and plan a review. Continue into the accommodation, digital standards or procurement courses where they fit your work.

scenario.context: In this example, a team repaired three documents and wants to report that its entire service is now accessible. It has not checked the form, confirmation or later response.
options: Say the whole service is accessible because three files were repaired.
Do not report any progress until every possible issue is solved.
Describe the three verified repairs, identify the unchecked steps and assign the next review.
responses: This extends the evidence beyond what was examined. It may hide the remaining barriers.
Completed repairs are worth reporting with their limits. Waiting for perfection can obscure both progress and responsibility.
This gives an honest account of progress and a clear next action. It does not claim universal compliance or diminish the completed work.

lessons.transfer: Write a brief update about a practice task: what was checked, what changed, what remains unknown and who will follow up. Leave personal medical information out.

move.control: You can ask for supported conclusions and make unresolved work visible.
move.failure: Training counts, silence or closed tickets are treated as proof of complete access.
move.next: Choose one review date and confirm the evidence you need to judge the task itself.

jobAid.subtitle: A leadership review for accessible work and services
remember: Start with a complete task and the person’s control over it.
Use accessible defaults and the appropriate individual response.
Employment medical information and accommodation status belong in the confidential agency process.
This learning routine does not replace required accessibility checks or formal decisions.

sections.heading: Before the decision
items: Name who uses the task and what they must be able to do from start to finish.
Identify the applicable responsibilities and the appropriate accessibility, accommodation or procurement contacts.
Include specialist time, testing, repair and follow-up in the plan.

sections.heading: At the review
items: Ask what was tested, under which conditions and against which requirements.
Consider participant experience without asking one person to represent a whole group.
Distinguish a report or promise from evidence that the configured task works.

sections.heading: After the change
items: Verify the correction and the complete task.
Describe progress and remaining gaps accurately.
Assign an owner and date to unresolved work and check back with affected people through the appropriate channel.
